claims.evidence: NHS says everyone should consider vitamin D in autumn and winter and folic acid is advised in early pregnancy, but no returned text calls these 'the main exceptions' to getting what is needed from diet (vitamin A, babies and young children are also covered).
claims.newSentence: The NHS says a varied and balanced diet should provide enough of several vitamins, but advises supplements for some people, including vitamin D in autumn and winter and folic acid in early pregnancy.

claims.evidence: nhs.uk Vitamin D page confirms everyone should consider a daily 10 microgram supplement in autumn and winter. 'Because it is hard to get enough from food alone' was not seen in any returned text.
claims.newSentence: NHS pages advise that everyone should consider taking a vitamin D supplement in autumn and winter.

claims.evidence: NHS inform: people seldom outdoors (frail, housebound, care home) and people of African, African-Caribbean and South Asian origin should take a daily supplement throughout the year. nhs.uk: people at high risk of not getting enough take it all year.
NHS pregnancy vitamins page: folic acid daily while trying to get pregnant (or as soon as pregnancy is found) until the 12th week. Sentence wording 'pregnant or could become pregnant' fits.
nhs.uk Vitamin D page: do not take more than 100 micrograms (4,000 IU) a day as it could be harmful.

Could not retrieve text saying supplements are recommended 'only' for some people and times of year. Retrieved: NHS says for vitamin A one should be able to get all needed from a varied balanced diet, and advises supplements for particular groups.
claims.newSentence: NHS pages say that a varied and balanced diet should provide all that is needed of some vitamins, such as vitamin A, while supplements are advised for some groups.

claims.evidence: 'Difficult to get enough from food alone' not seen in returned text. Retrieved from nhs.uk Vitamin D: most people can make all the vitamin D they need from sunlight on skin from about late March/early April to end of September.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says that from about late March or early April to the end of September, most people can make the vitamin D they need from sunlight on the skin.

claims.evidence: nhs.uk Vitamin D: everyone (including pregnant and breastfeeding women) should consider a daily 10 microgram supplement during autumn and winter.

No source says seasonal advice 'starts at age 4' in England or 'age 5' in Scotland. nhs.uk: all babies and children aged 1 to 4 should take a supplement all year; everyone should consider it in autumn and winter. NHS inform lists babies and children under 5 as a higher-risk group. The ages are year-round-advice ages, not the start of seasonal advice. Age groups differ in wording (1 to 4 vs under 5), not in substance.
claims.newSentence: In England the NHS advises all babies and children aged 1 to 4 to take vitamin D throughout the year, and NHS inform in Scotland describes babies and children under 5 as a higher-risk group.

claims.evidence: NHS inform vitamin D and vitamins pages: people seldom outdoors (frail, housebound, care home), people who usually cover most of their skin outdoors, and people of African, African-Caribbean or South Asian origin take 10 micrograms daily all year. Ledger cited NHS 111 Wales; NHS inform carried it in the retrieval.

nhs.uk Vitamin D: breastfed babies from birth to 1 year have a daily supplement all year; all children aged 1 to 4 take it throughout the year. Formula-fed babies are exempt only if they have more than 500ml formula a day (not mentioned in the sentence, which concerns breastfed babies).
Healthy Start site: people on the scheme are entitled to free Healthy Start vitamins (drops for babies/children up to their 4th birthday; tablets for pregnancy and breastfeeding).
NHS pregnancy page: 400 micrograms folic acid daily when trying to get pregnant and until 12 weeks; taking longer will not harm the baby.
NHS pregnancy page lists diabetes and epilepsy medicine among reasons for a higher (5mg) dose, prescribed by a GP; epilepsy page says to take 5mg once a day from when trying to get pregnant.

nhs.uk Vitamin D: do not take more than 100 micrograms a day as it could be harmful; applies to adults including pregnant and breastfeeding women and the elderly, and children aged 11 to 17. Children aged 1 to 10 not named in that statement (sentence correctly omits them).

Returned text: 1mg or less a day of folic acid is unlikely to cause harm; higher doses can mask vitamin B12 deficiency. 'Too much could be harmful' in general terms was not seen. Reworded to the retrieved statement.
claims.newSentence: For folic acid, the NHS says 1 milligram or less a day of supplements is unlikely to cause any harm, and that higher doses can mask the symptoms of vitamin B12 deficiency.

claims.evidence: No returned text listed the vitamins and minerals the NHS guide covers. Low-value sentence.
Vitamin A: NHS says you should be able to get all you need from a varied and balanced diet (retrieved). The same wording for iron was not seen in returned text.
claims.newSentence: For vitamin A, the NHS says most people should be able to get all they need from a varied and balanced diet.

claims.evidence: 'Helps regulate the amount of calcium and phosphate in the body' confirmed on nhs.uk Vitamin D. 'Sunlight is the main source' was not stated in returned text; only that most people can make it from sunlight in spring and summer.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says vitamin D helps regulate the amount of calcium and phosphate in the body.

claims.evidence: nhs.uk Vitamin D: from about late March or early April to the end of September, most people can make all the vitamin D they need from sunlight on the skin.
NHS 111 Wales vitamins and minerals page: iron is important in making red blood cells, which carry oxygen around the body.

NHS 111 Wales: liver is very rich in vitamin A and liver or liver products such as pâté should not be eaten more than once a week. NHS pregnancy page and NHS Scotland: people who are pregnant are advised to avoid liver and liver products and vitamin A supplements. In a guide that discusses pregnancy, the once-a-week wording alone could mislead.
claims.newSentence: Liver is very rich in vitamin A; the NHS says liver or liver products such as pâté should not be eaten more than once a week, and advises people who are pregnant to avoid them.

notes: Age/group wording: c09 was the one clear error (invented 'starts at age 4/5'). England wording is 'all babies and children aged 1 to 4 year-round'; Scotland frames under-5s. The England vs Scotland groups are otherwise equivalent in the pages retrieved. Some local NHS documents list people aged 65 and over as a year-round group; the nhs.uk Vitamin D page did not in the returned text, so the guide's omission is fine but the 65+ point should not be added without checking. Doses: c02, c08, c13, c15, c16 carry numeric doses (10, 400, 100 micrograms, 1 mg) which conflict with the site rule 'no doses in prose'; caller may want to move them to records. Folic acid dose and timing (400 micrograms until week 12; higher 5mg dose via GP for diabetes or epilepsy medicine) confirmed. Vitamin A and liver: once-a-week wording confirmed from NHS 111 Wales; pregnancy avoidance confirmed from NHS pages. Several ledger URLs (NHS 111 Wales) were not the page that carried the statement; the nhs.uk Vitamin D page and NHS inform did. The search tool blends pages, so the NHS 111 Wales attributions are moderately confident.
